buildUp: Start with the goal: shrink a chip pattern four times and print it onto a wafer, with smaller details than 193 nm light can manage. That means a shorter wavelength, and the best mirrors available reflect around 13.5 nm, so that's the wavelength.

No lamp makes useful amounts of 13.5 nm light, so make a tiny, very hot plasma instead. Fire molten tin droplets across a vessel and hit each one with a powerful CO2 laser, first to flatten it, then to blow it into a glowing plasma, 50,000 times a second.

The plasma glows in all directions, so put a large ellipse-shaped multilayer mirror behind it to collect as much as possible and focus it through a small opening, the intermediate focus. Fill the vessel with hydrogen to keep tin off the mirror.
The light from the source is uneven, so an illuminator of faceted mirrors chops it into slices and overlaps them into an evenly lit slit, arriving from the angles that print each pattern best.

Glass absorbs EUV, so the mask has to be a mirror too: a multilayer reflector with the circuit drawn on top in an absorbing metal. The light hits it at a slight angle so the reflection heads down into the projection optics.
Six precisely shaped mirrors shrink the pattern four times onto the wafer. Each loses about 30% of the light, so the source must be bright and the mirrors must be the smoothest ever made.

The slit only covers a strip, so the reticle and wafer scan through it together in perfect step. A second wafer stage measures the next wafer while the first is exposed, and a separate quiet frame keeps every measurement steady to a fraction of a nanometre.
firstPrinciples.coreIdea: Switch to light with a wavelength of just 13.5 nm, fourteen times shorter than before, so the same projection trick can print far finer patterns. That light is absorbed by almost everything, so the whole machine has to be rebuilt around it: no air, no lenses, only mirrors, and a light source that makes the light by blasting molten tin into plasma 50,000 times a second.

hardParts.title: Making enough light
hardParts.why: Only a few per cent of the laser's energy comes out as usable EUV, and each of the roughly ten mirrors afterwards keeps only about 70%. Getting a couple of hundred watts of EUV to the intermediate focus means hitting tiny, fast-moving droplets perfectly 50,000 times a second, with a laser of tens of kilowatts, for months on end. For about two decades the source was too weak, and EUV seemed it might never reach the factory.

hardParts.title: Keeping the collector clean
hardParts.why: The collector mirror sits only centimetres from an exploding tin plasma, yet a coating of tin just a few nanometres thick would ruin its reflection. Debris shields, hydrogen gas that turns tin into a vapour to be pumped away, and careful control of the plasma all have to work together so the mirror lasts for months.

hardParts.title: Mirrors smooth and still to the atom
hardParts.why: Any bump or tilt in the projection mirrors blurs the image, and the tolerances are a fraction of a nanometre over surfaces tens of centimetres across. Zeiss polishes, measures and coats them over many months, and then the mirrors must hold their shape and position while the light warms them, inside a vacuum, while stages race about nearby.

principles.explanation: Light spreads out a little whenever it passes through an opening or round an edge, which blurs any detail smaller than roughly its wavelength. The smallest feature a projector can print is about the wavelength divided by twice the numerical aperture, a measure of how wide a cone of light the optics collect. You can widen the cone, but there's a limit, so the big lever is the wavelength. Going from 193 nm to 13.5 nm makes much smaller features printable in a single exposure.
principles.title: Shorter waves draw finer lines

principles.explanation: EUV light is absorbed by almost anything it meets, so the machine can have no lenses and the entire light path, from the plasma to the wafer, has to be in vacuum. Photons of 13.5 nm light carry about 92 electronvolts each, enough to knock electrons out of almost any atom they meet. So instead of passing through, they're absorbed within a tiny distance: a few centimetres of air, or a fraction of a micrometre of glass.
principles.title: EUV is swallowed by everything

principles.explanation: No single surface reflects EUV well, but a stack of about 40 alternating layers sends back tiny reflections that add up in step, giving about 70% reflection. A single polished surface reflects almost no EUV at a steep angle. But stack alternating layers of molybdenum and silicon, each pair about 7 nm thick, half the wavelength, and the tiny reflection from every boundary comes back in step with the others. They add up like waves in sync. It's the same reason a soap bubble shows bright colours.
principles.title: Many weak reflections add up

principles.explanation: The machine makes its EUV light by heating tin into a plasma, because only something extremely hot glows at such short wavelengths. The hotter something is, the shorter the wavelengths it gives off: a stove glows red, the Sun glows yellow-white. To glow in extreme ultraviolet you need hundreds of thousands of degrees. Tin is ideal because its highly charged ions happen to emit very strongly in a narrow band around 13.5 nm, matching the mirrors' best reflection.
principles.title: Hot plasma glows at short wavelengths

firstPrinciples.problem: Print billions of transistors on a sliver of silicon, with lines only a few tens of atoms wide, and do it on a hundred-odd wafers an hour without a single misplaced layer. Chips are made by projecting a pattern of light onto a light-sensitive coating, but light can't draw details much smaller than its own wavelength, and the deep-ultraviolet light the industry used for decades had run out of room to shrink.

questions.answer: EUV light is absorbed by almost any material, including glass, within a tiny distance. Lenses would simply soak it up. Multilayer mirrors can reflect about 70% of it, so the whole optical path is built from mirrors, and in vacuum, because air absorbs it too.
questions.question: Why does an EUV machine use only mirrors, when older chipmaking machines used big glass lenses?

questions.answer: A weak first pulse flattens the round droplet into a thin pancake. That gives the powerful main pulse a larger, better-shaped target, so more of its energy is turned into EUV light and less tin is wasted as debris.
questions.question: Why does each tin droplet get hit by the laser twice?

questions.answer: Before exposure, each wafer has to be measured carefully, both where the earlier layers are and how its surface rises and falls. Doing that on one stage while the other exposes means no time is lost, so the machine prints more wafers an hour and can afford to measure more thoroughly.
questions.question: Why does the machine need two wafer stages?

firstPrinciples.xFactor: EUV wasn't one invention but thousands of them working together, from atom-thin mirror coatings to a laser that hits droplets mid-flight and stages that move in perfect step at several g. ASML's real breakthrough was organising it: spending decades and billions with partners like Zeiss, Trumpf and its own Cymer, sharing the risk with chipmakers such as Intel, TSMC and Samsung who invested in it, and refusing to give up when the source seemed impossible. That's why only one company in the world can build these machines.

name: EUV Lithography Machine
overview:
Every advanced chip in a modern phone or AI data centre has its finest layers printed by one of these machines. They work like an enormous slide projector run backwards: a pattern on a mask, called the reticle, is shrunk four times and projected onto a silicon wafer coated with light-sensitive resist. The smaller the wavelength of the light, the finer the detail you can print, so the industry moved from 193 nm deep-ultraviolet light to extreme ultraviolet at just 13.5 nm. Only one company, the Dutch firm ASML, makes them, with mirrors from Zeiss in Germany and a drive laser from Trumpf.

EUV light is absorbed by almost everything, including air and glass, so the whole light path sits in vacuum and there are no lenses at all, only mirrors. To make the light, a droplet generator fires about 50,000 tiny drops of molten tin every second. A powerful CO2 laser hits each drop twice: a weak pulse flattens it into a pancake, then a strong one turns it into a plasma hotter than the surface of the Sun, which glows in EUV. A large curved collector mirror gathers that glow and focuses it to a point, the intermediate focus, where it enters the scanner.

From there an illuminator of faceted mirrors shapes the light into an even slit and shines it onto the reticle, which is itself a mirror with the chip pattern drawn on it in absorbing metal. Six more mirrors in the projection optics shrink the reflected pattern onto the wafer. While it exposes, the reticle and wafer race past each other in perfect step, and a second wafer stage measures the next wafer so no time is wasted. Each mirror reflects only about 70% of the light, so after roughly ten bounces only a few per cent reaches the wafer, which is why the source has to be so bright.

parts.description: White roof panel over the whole scanner; like all the covers it keeps dust out and lifts off for service.

details.didYouKnow: A whole EUV machine is shipped in pieces, in about 40 freight containers, on around 20 lorries and 3 cargo jets, and it takes months to put together again in the chip factory.
details.howItWorks: The roof of the machine is a set of white panels that keep dust, light and stray air currents away from the modules underneath. It isn't structural and carries no load; it simply lifts away so engineers and cranes can reach the optics and stages. Inside, the machine also keeps its own temperature steady, because even a fraction of a degree of change would make parts grow and shrink by more than the features being printed.
keyNumbers: Whole scanner roughly the size of a city bus
Around 3 m tall in the cleanroom
Machine weighs roughly 150 to 180 tonnes
details.madeOf: Painted sheet steel and aluminium panels on a light frame, finished in the plain white of a cleanroom tool.

parts.name: Top cover

parts.description: Left half of the white front panels; behind them sits a vacuum vessel, not a cabinet of air.

details.didYouKnow: ASML, from Veldhoven in the Netherlands, is the only company in the world that makes EUV machines. Rivals such as Nikon and Canon dropped out long before EUV reached the factory floor.
details.howItWorks: The front panels are the face of the machine that people in the cleanroom see, usually with ASML's name and a small status screen on them. Behind the left-hand half sits the light source end of the machine. Taking them off is the first step in any service visit, and the panels are designed to come away without disturbing anything inside.
keyNumbers: Panels a few millimetres thick
Cleanroom air around the machine has far fewer dust particles than ordinary air
Covers a machine roughly 4 m deep
details.madeOf: Powder-coated steel or aluminium sheet with seals round the edges, held on by quick-release fixings.

parts.name: Front cover (left)

parts.description: Right half of the front panels, which open for service engineers to reach the stages.

details.didYouKnow: Engineers wear full cleanroom 'bunny suits' when they open the machine, because a single skin flake on a mirror or reticle could ruin thousands of chips.
details.howItWorks: The right-hand front panels close off the end of the machine where wafers come in and go out. That end connects straight to a 'track', a separate machine that coats wafers in light-sensitive resist before exposure and develops them afterwards, so the panels here also seal the link between the two.
keyNumbers: Works alongside a coating and developing track
Wafers pass through in well under a minute each
About 160 wafers an hour on recent models
details.madeOf: Painted metal sheet with seals and service hatches, matching the rest of the white covers.

parts.name: Front cover (right)

parts.description: End panels at each end of the scanner; the beam from the drive laser comes in through the left one.

details.didYouKnow: Most of the megawatt an EUV machine draws ends up as heat in the drive laser and the source, so it needs serious cooling, more like a small industrial plant than an office machine.
details.howItWorks: End panels close off the two short sides of the scanner. In a real factory the CO2 laser usually sits on the floor below, and its beam comes up through the floor into the source end, so the side covers there have openings and seals for the beam line, cables and cooling water.
keyNumbers: 2 end panels
Machine uses roughly a megawatt of electricity
Openings for the laser beam line, cables and cooling water
details.madeOf: Painted metal panels with gaskets, matching the front and top covers.

parts.name: Side covers

parts.description: Steel vessel round the illuminator, reticle, projection optics and wafer stages, pumped down because air swallows EUV light.

details.didYouKnow: The mirrors are so sensitive that a layer of contamination only a nanometre or so thick, a few atoms, measurably cuts the light reaching the wafer, which is why the vacuum has to be kept so clean.
details.howItWorks: EUV light is absorbed by almost everything, including a few centimetres of air, so the whole path from the source to the wafer runs in vacuum. Pumps draw the chamber down, and a little very-low-pressure hydrogen is let in on purpose: it barely absorbs EUV and helps scrub carbon and tin off the mirrors. Load-locks let reticles and wafers in and out without letting air into the main chamber.
keyNumbers: Pressure many thousands of times lower than air
Light travels several metres in vacuum
Separate vacuum zones for the source, optics and stages
details.madeOf: Thick stainless-steel walls with machined flanges and seals, fitted with turbomolecular pumps that spin at tens of thousands of rpm.

parts.name: Vacuum chamber

parts.description: Heavy welded frame that carries the modules; it shakes as the stages race about, so the optics hang from a separate quiet frame.

details.didYouKnow: Some of the force from the stages is soaked up by balance masses that move the opposite way, like a recoiling gun, so less vibration reaches the factory floor.
details.howItWorks: The main frame is the skeleton the modules hang on: the source vessel, the illuminator, the stages and their motors. When the stages accelerate, their motors push back against something, and that force goes into this frame. That's fine here, because the precise optics and the measuring systems sit on a separate, quiet frame that never feels those shakes.
keyNumbers: Carries modules weighing many tonnes
Takes the reaction forces from stages moving at several g
Part of a machine of roughly 150 to 180 tonnes
details.madeOf: Welded and bolted steel sections, very stiff and heavy, with mounts for the modules and channels for cables and water.

parts.name: Main frame

parts.description: Ultra-stiff frame on soft air mounts that the mirrors and sensors are measured from, isolated from the shaking main frame.

details.didYouKnow: Separating a 'force frame' from a 'metrology frame' is an old trick from precision engineering: one frame takes the pushing, the other does the measuring, so nothing that is pushed is ever used as a ruler.
details.howItWorks: Every measurement of where the reticle and wafer are is made relative to this frame, so it has to stay absolutely still. It floats on soft air mounts and active actuators that cancel out vibration from the floor and the main frame. Sensors on it watch the stages through encoder grids and interferometers, so their positions are known to well below a nanometre.
keyNumbers: Positions measured to a fraction of a nanometre
Temperature held to within a few thousandths of a degree in critical places
Isolated from vibration by air mounts
details.madeOf: Materials chosen for stiffness and tiny thermal expansion, such as special ceramics or low-expansion alloys, kept at a tightly controlled temperature.

parts.name: Isolated metrology frame

parts.description: Massive base the whole scanner stands on, spreading its weight of well over 100 tonnes across the fab floor.

details.didYouKnow: Chip factories are built on massive concrete slabs, separated from the rest of the building, so lorries, wind and even footsteps don't shake the scanners.
details.howItWorks: The base frame spreads the enormous weight of the scanner across the factory floor and gives everything a level, rigid foundation to stand on. In a chip fab the cleanroom floor is often a raised grating over a 'subfab' below, where lasers, pumps and power supplies live, and the base frame sits on a stiff pedestal that runs down through it.
keyNumbers: Supports a machine of roughly 150 to 180 tonnes
Roughly the size of a bus
Floor must stay level to tiny tolerances
details.madeOf: Heavy welded steel or cast sections, levelled on adjustable feet.

parts.name: Base frame

parts.description: Trumpf-built carbon-dioxide laser the size of a small room, in the floor below, firing pulses of infrared light at the tin.

details.didYouKnow: The CO2 laser was chosen partly because its long infrared wavelength makes the tin plasma convert energy into EUV more efficiently than shorter-wavelength lasers do. Even so, only a few per cent of the laser's energy comes out as useful EUV light.
details.howItWorks: A small seed laser makes weak, precisely timed pulses, and a chain of amplifiers full of glowing carbon-dioxide gas multiplies them into a beam of tens of kilowatts. Each tin droplet is hit twice: a small 'pre-pulse' flattens it into a thin pancake, and microseconds later the main pulse turns the pancake into a plasma. The laser usually sits in the subfab beneath the scanner and its beam is piped up through the floor.
keyNumbers: Infrared light at 10.6 micrometres
Average power in the tens of kilowatts
Fires about 50,000 pairs of pulses a second
details.madeOf: Built by the German company Trumpf: gas-filled amplifier tubes, water-cooled electrodes, big copper mirrors and a lot of power electronics, adding up to hundreds of thousands of parts.

parts.name: CO2 drive laser

parts.description: Sealed tube of mirrors that carries the laser beam from the laser into the back of the source vessel.

details.didYouKnow: Infrared at 10.6 micrometres passes straight through some materials that look opaque, such as zinc selenide, which glows yellow-orange to the eye but is used as 'glass' for CO2 laser windows and lenses.
details.howItWorks: The beam transport carries the laser's invisible infrared beam from the laser up into the source vessel. Inside the tube, mirrors steer the beam round corners, and a final focusing optic squeezes it to a tiny spot at exactly the place where the droplets fly past. Sensors check its position constantly, because the spot has to land on a droplet only tens of micrometres across.
keyNumbers: Carries tens of kilowatts of infrared light
Several metres long
Focuses to a spot only tens of micrometres wide
details.madeOf: Sealed metal ducts holding water-cooled copper or coated mirrors, with beam-position sensors along the way.

parts.name: Beam transport

parts.description: Cone-shaped vacuum vessel where the tin is turned into plasma; hydrogen gas inside sweeps stray tin away from the mirror.

details.didYouKnow: Making a bright, reliable EUV source was the biggest obstacle to the whole technology for about two decades. Early sources gave only a few watts, far too little to print wafers at a useful speed.
details.howItWorks: The source vessel is where the light is made. Inside it, tin droplets fly through the laser's focus, flash into plasma and glow in EUV. The trouble is that every flash also sprays tin, so the vessel is filled with low-pressure hydrogen flowing past the collector. The hydrogen slows down tin atoms and turns tin deposits into a gas that can be pumped away, keeping the mirror clean.
keyNumbers: Around 250 W of EUV at the intermediate focus on recent models
Hydrogen at a small fraction of atmospheric pressure
Collector swapped after long service intervals
details.madeOf: Stainless steel, water-cooled, with ports for the laser, droplet generator, catcher, hydrogen flow, pumps and many sensors. The source is developed largely by Cymer, ASML's subsidiary in San Diego.

parts.name: Source vessel

parts.description: Nozzle that squirts about 50,000 droplets of molten tin a second, each about 30 micrometres across.

details.didYouKnow: Tin was picked because tin ions happen to glow very strongly in a narrow band right around 13.5 nm, exactly where the best mirrors reflect.
details.howItWorks: A reservoir of tin, melted at about 250 °C, is pushed through a tiny nozzle by high-pressure gas. A vibrating piezo crystal breaks the jet into a perfectly regular stream of droplets, all the same size and evenly spaced, so the laser can be timed to hit each one. Droplets the laser misses fly on into a catcher on the far side.
keyNumbers: About 50,000 droplets a second
Each droplet about 25 to 30 micrometres across
Droplets fly at roughly 70 to 80 metres a second
details.madeOf: A heated steel reservoir and a nozzle with a hole only micrometres across, driven by a piezoelectric actuator.

parts.name: Tin droplet generator

parts.description: Stream of falling-fast tin droplets crossing the laser's focus; the ones not hit end up in a catcher on the far side.

details.didYouKnow: Hitting a droplet the width of a hair, flying at about 70 m/s, 50,000 times a second, is often compared to hitting a moving pea with a laser from across a room, again and again without a miss.
details.howItWorks: The droplets fly across the vessel in a straight line, and cameras track every one so the laser can fire at exactly the right moment and spot. Each droplet is hit first by a pre-pulse that squashes it into a disc a fraction of a millimetre wide, giving the main pulse a bigger target, then by the main pulse that vaporises it into plasma.
keyNumbers: 50,000 droplets a second
Hit twice each, by a pre-pulse and a main pulse
Only a few milligrams of tin used per second
details.madeOf: Pure molten tin, the same metal used in solder.

parts.name: Tin droplet stream

parts.description: The infrared laser pulses, fired through a hole in the middle of the collector to hit each droplet twice.

details.didYouKnow: If you scaled the droplet up to a football, the laser would still need to hit it every time, 50,000 times a second, and that's after the beam has travelled several metres from the floor below.
details.howItWorks: The laser pulses arrive through a hole in the middle of the collector mirror and are focused onto the droplet stream. Pulses come in pairs: a gentle pre-pulse first, then the powerful main pulse just after. The timing between them is adjusted so the tin pancake is the ideal shape when the main pulse lands.
keyNumbers: Wavelength 10.6 micrometres
About 50,000 pulse pairs a second
Each main pulse lasts only tens of nanoseconds
details.madeOf: Infrared light from a carbon-dioxide laser, invisible to the eye and drawn here in red.

parts.name: Laser beam

parts.description: Spot where a flattened droplet becomes a plasma of around 200,000 °C that glows in 13.5 nm light.

details.didYouKnow: 13.5 nm light sits between ultraviolet and X-rays. It's about 14 times shorter in wavelength than the 193 nm deep-ultraviolet light used by the previous generation of scanners.
details.howItWorks: The main laser pulse heats the tin so fast that its atoms lose many electrons, forming a tiny ball of plasma. As electrons drop back into tin ions they give off light, and tin ions happen to glow brightly at 13.5 nm. The flash lasts a moment and then the next droplet arrives, so the source is really a strobe flashing 50,000 times a second.
keyNumbers: Roughly 200,000 °C, around 40 times hotter than the Sun's surface
Light at 13.5 nm, extreme ultraviolet
Only a few per cent of the laser energy becomes useful EUV
details.madeOf: Highly charged tin ions and free electrons, a fraction of a millimetre across.

parts.name: Tin plasma

parts.description: Large dished multilayer mirror behind the plasma that gathers its EUV glow and focuses it onwards.

details.didYouKnow: The collector faces a constant spray of tin, so keeping it clean is one of the hardest jobs in the machine. The flow of hydrogen gas across it, which turns tin deposits into a gas, is what makes it last for months rather than minutes.
details.howItWorks: The collector is a big dish shaped like part of an ellipse. An ellipse has two focus points, and light leaving one focus is reflected to the other, so with the plasma at the first focus all the EUV it catches is sent to a point further on, the intermediate focus. Its surface is a stack of alternating molybdenum and silicon layers that reflect EUV, because ordinary metal mirrors don't.
keyNumbers: Roughly 60 to 70 cm across
Reflects roughly half of the EUV that reaches it
Sits only tens of centimetres from a 200,000 °C plasma
details.madeOf: A precisely shaped substrate coated with around 40 pairs of molybdenum and silicon layers, each pair about 7 nm thick, plus a protective cap.

parts.name: Collector mirror

parts.description: Small opening where the collected light is squeezed to a point and handed over from the source to the scanner.

details.didYouKnow: Because each of the roughly ten mirrors after this point reflects only about 70% of the light, the 250 W at the intermediate focus becomes just a few watts at the wafer.
details.howItWorks: The intermediate focus is where the collector brings all the EUV light to a point, a few millimetres across. It's the doorway between the dirty source and the clean scanner: a small opening means very little tin or gas can get through, while all the light can. Power here is the standard way of measuring how bright an EUV source is.
keyNumbers: Spot a few millimetres across
Around 250 W of EUV passes through on recent models
Separates the source vacuum from the scanner vacuum
details.madeOf: A cooled metal aperture with gas flows round it that act as a barrier to debris.

parts.name: Intermediate focus

parts.description: The 13.5 nm light on its way from the plasma to the intermediate focus; invisible to the eye, drawn here in violet.

details.didYouKnow: EUV photons carry so much energy that they knock electrons out of almost anything they hit, which is why the light can't pass through any lens and the whole machine is built from mirrors.
details.howItWorks: This is the EUV light leaving the plasma, bouncing off the collector and converging on the intermediate focus. In reality it's a broad cone of light filling the vessel, drawn here as a single line through the centre. EUV is completely invisible to the eye.
keyNumbers: Wavelength 13.5 nm
Photon energy about 92 electronvolts
Absorbed by a few centimetres of air
details.madeOf: Extreme-ultraviolet light at 13.5 nm, drawn in violet.

parts.name: EUV light (source)

parts.description: Vacuum box that holds the illuminator's mirrors rigidly in line between the source and the reticle.

details.didYouKnow: Different chip layers print better with light arriving from different angles, such as a ring or two or four poles of light. The illuminator can switch between these patterns in seconds.
details.howItWorks: The illuminator takes the uneven blob of light from the source and turns it into an evenly lit curved slit, hitting the reticle from exactly the right angles. This housing holds its mirrors in vacuum and keeps them aligned while heat from the light warms them up. Motors inside can retilt mirror facets to change the lighting pattern for each chip layer.
keyNumbers: 4 mirrors in this model
Turns the light into a slit about 26 mm wide at the wafer
Mirrors reflect about 70% each
details.madeOf: A stiff metal vacuum housing with water cooling and mounts for the mirrors, built by Zeiss.

parts.name: Illuminator housing

parts.description: Mirror made of hundreds of small tilted facets that chops the beam into slices and overlaps them into an even slit.

details.didYouKnow: This 'fly's eye' trick of chopping light into many overlapping images has been used in projectors for decades. In an EUV machine it has to be done with mirrors instead of lens arrays.
details.howItWorks: This mirror is made of hundreds of small curved facets, each catching a slice of the beam. Every facet images its slice onto the reticle, and because all the slices overlap there, any bright or dark patches in the source average out. The result is a slit of light that's equally bright from one end to the other.
keyNumbers: Hundreds of facets
Each multilayer about 40 molybdenum-silicon pairs
Evens out bright and dark patches in the beam
details.madeOf: Hundreds of small multilayer-coated mirror facets on a cooled base, many of them tiltable by tiny actuators.

parts.name: Field facet mirror

parts.description: Second faceted mirror that sets the angles the light arrives at the reticle from, matched to each chip layer.

details.didYouKnow: Choosing the best light angles for a pattern is now worked out by computer, together with tweaks to the mask pattern itself, in a method called source-mask optimisation.
details.howItWorks: Each field facet sends its slice of light to a facet on this second mirror. Where those facets sit decides the angles from which the light reaches the reticle, called the illumination pupil. By tilting field facets to aim at different pupil facets, the machine can light the reticle from a ring, from two poles or from four, whichever prints a given pattern best.
keyNumbers: Hundreds of facets
Settings changed for each chip layer
Reflects about 70% of the light
details.madeOf: Many small multilayer-coated mirror facets arranged on a disc-shaped mount.

parts.name: Pupil facet mirror

parts.description: Curved mirror that gathers the light from the facet mirrors and shapes it into the exposure slit.

details.didYouKnow: A multilayer mirror works like the colours on a soap bubble: tiny reflections from each of the many layer boundaries all line up in step at one wavelength, adding up to a strong reflection.
details.howItWorks: The condenser gathers the light coming off the pupil facets and directs it onwards so the slit lands in exactly the right place and size. Its curved surface helps shape the slit into the gentle arc that the projection optics are designed to use.
keyNumbers: About 40 molybdenum-silicon layer pairs
Reflects about 70% at 13.5 nm
Shape accurate to a fraction of a nanometre
details.madeOf: A precision-polished low-expansion glass-ceramic substrate with a molybdenum-silicon multilayer coating.

parts.name: Condenser mirror

parts.description: Last illuminator mirror, struck at a shallow angle, that steers the slit up onto the reticle.

details.didYouKnow: X-ray telescopes in space use the same grazing-incidence trick, nesting long, shallow mirrors inside each other because X-rays won't reflect off mirrors at steep angles.
details.howItWorks: The light hits this mirror at a shallow, glancing angle, like a stone skipping on water. At such angles, smooth metal surfaces reflect EUV well even without a multilayer coating, so it can steer the slit up onto the reticle with little loss.
keyNumbers: Light arrives at a shallow angle
Can reflect more than a multilayer mirror at this angle
Last mirror before the reticle
details.madeOf: A smooth polished substrate with a thin metal coating such as ruthenium.

parts.name: Grazing-incidence mirror

parts.description: The light zig-zagging through the illuminator's four mirrors on its way up to the reticle.

details.didYouKnow: The light can't hit the reticle straight on, because a reflective mask would send it straight back into the illuminator. Tilting it by about 6 degrees lets the reflected beam head off into the projection optics instead.
details.howItWorks: The light enters at the intermediate focus, zig-zags off the field facet mirror, the pupil facet mirror, the condenser and the grazing-incidence mirror, then strikes the reticle at a slight angle. In reality it is a wide, carefully shaped bundle of light, drawn here as a single line.
keyNumbers: 4 reflections in this model
Loses roughly a quarter or more at each multilayer bounce
Arrives at the reticle about 6 degrees off vertical
details.madeOf: Extreme-ultraviolet light at 13.5 nm, drawn in violet.

parts.name: EUV light (illuminator)

parts.description: Magnetically levitated stage that holds the reticle upside down and sweeps it through the light at high speed.

details.didYouKnow: During each scan the reticle and wafer move in opposite directions, because the projection optics turn the image upside down, just as a camera lens does.
details.howItWorks: The reticle stage holds the mask upside down and sweeps it through the slit of light while the wafer stage sweeps the wafer the other way below. Because the image is four times smaller at the wafer, the reticle has to move four times faster and further. It floats on magnetic fields, holds the mask with an electrostatic clamp because vacuum suction doesn't work in a vacuum, and is tracked to well below a nanometre.
keyNumbers: Moves 4 times faster than the wafer stage
Accelerates at many times the force of gravity
Synchronised with the wafer stage to the nanometre
details.madeOf: Lightweight, very stiff ceramic and metal parts, driven by linear motors and levitated magnetically, with position encoders.

parts.name: Reticle stage

parts.description: The master pattern for one chip layer: a mirror-coated plate with the circuit drawn on it in absorbing metal.

details.didYouKnow: A single speck of dust on an EUV mask would be printed onto every chip it exposes. Masks can be protected by a pellicle, a membrane only tens of nanometres thick held a few millimetres above the pattern, which keeps dust out of focus.
details.howItWorks: The reticle, or mask, carries the pattern for one layer of a chip at four times its final size. Unlike older masks, which light shone through, an EUV mask is a mirror: a multilayer stack reflects the light, and a patterned absorbing layer on top blocks it wherever there should be no line on the chip. Each chip needs dozens of layers, so a chip design needs a whole set of masks.
keyNumbers: 152 mm square and about 6.35 mm thick
Pattern drawn 4 times larger than on the wafer
Exposure field 26 x 33 mm on the wafer
details.madeOf: A thick plate of ultra-low-expansion glass, coated with about 40 molybdenum-silicon pairs and a patterned absorber, often based on tantalum.

parts.name: Reticle (mask)

parts.description: Robot and vacuum load-lock that swaps reticles in and out from their sealed pods without letting in a speck of dust.

details.didYouKnow: Because EUV masks are so valuable and so sensitive to contamination, they are often checked by separate inspection machines that look for defects only a few tens of nanometres across.
details.howItWorks: Reticles arrive at the machine sealed in special double pods. The handler opens them, passes the reticle through a load-lock into the vacuum, checks it for particles and hands it to the stage, all with robots, because no human hand ever touches a mask. It keeps a small library of reticles so switching between layers or products is quick.
keyNumbers: Stores several reticles
Each mask can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars
Swaps a reticle in a minute or two
details.madeOf: Vacuum robots, load-lock chambers, an inspection camera and storage racks inside a sealed housing.

parts.name: Reticle handler

parts.description: Zeiss-built housing that holds the six projection mirrors in place to within a fraction of a nanometre.

details.didYouKnow: Zeiss has said that if one of these mirrors were blown up to the size of Germany, its biggest bump would be only about a tenth of a millimetre high.
details.howItWorks: The projection optics box holds the six mirrors that turn the reflected pattern into a four-times-smaller image on the wafer. Any movement of a mirror would blur or shift that image, so the box is built to be extraordinarily stable, and sensors and tiny actuators keep each mirror exactly in place while the light warms it.
keyNumbers: 6 mirrors
Numerical aperture 0.33 on NXE machines
Prints lines down to about 13 nm
details.madeOf: Built by Zeiss in Oberkochen, Germany: a very stiff frame of low-expansion materials, mirror mounts with actuators, and cooling, all in vacuum.

parts.name: Projection optics box

parts.description: First projection mirror, catching the patterned light as it reflects down off the reticle.

details.didYouKnow: The layers in a multilayer mirror are each only a few nanometres thick, about the thickness of 15 to 20 atoms, and dozens must be laid down perfectly evenly across the whole mirror.
details.howItWorks: M1 catches the light reflected off the reticle, now carrying the chip pattern, and starts the job of reshaping it into a sharp image. Each of the six mirrors has a carefully calculated curved, non-spherical shape, and only together do they make an image free of blur and distortion across the whole slit.
keyNumbers: Reflects about 70% of the light
Surface roughness well below a nanometre
Shape correct to a fraction of a nanometre
details.madeOf: A low-expansion glass-ceramic substrate polished to atomic smoothness, coated with about 40 molybdenum-silicon layer pairs.

parts.name: Projection mirror M1

parts.description: Second mirror, folding the beam back across the optics box.

details.didYouKnow: The substrates are made of materials that barely change size with temperature, because a mirror that grew by even a few atoms as it warmed would visibly blur the image.
details.howItWorks: M2 folds the beam back across the optics box. The zig-zag layout keeps the mirrors out of each other's way while giving the light the path length it needs, so no mirror blocks the light heading to another.
keyNumbers: About 70% reflection
Multilayer pairs each about 7 nm thick
Held in place to within nanometres
details.madeOf: A polished low-expansion substrate with a molybdenum-silicon multilayer coating.

parts.name: Projection mirror M2

parts.description: Third mirror; together the six mirrors shrink the pattern four times.

details.didYouKnow: Polishing and measuring a single EUV mirror can take many months, and the measuring instruments themselves are among the most accurate ever built.
details.howItWorks: M3 is one of the mirrors near the middle of the system, where the beam is wide. Together with the others it brings rays from every point on the reticle back together at a matching point on the wafer, four times closer together.
keyNumbers: Reduction of 4 times
About 70% reflection
Kept at a steady temperature by cooling
details.madeOf: A polished low-expansion glass-ceramic blank with a molybdenum-silicon multilayer coating.

parts.name: Projection mirror M3

parts.description: Fourth mirror, one of the most precisely shaped surfaces ever made.

details.didYouKnow: After six projection mirrors, each reflecting roughly 70%, only about an eighth of the light leaving the reticle reaches the wafer.
details.howItWorks: M4 continues bending the light towards the wafer. Some of the mirrors in the box can be moved and bent very slightly by actuators, so the machine can correct small image errors that build up as the mirrors heat during long runs.
keyNumbers: About 70% reflection
Adjustable by tiny actuators
Corrections of a fraction of a nanometre
details.madeOf: A precision-polished low-expansion substrate with a multilayer coating, on an actively adjusted mount.

parts.name: Projection mirror M4

parts.description: Fifth mirror, small and close to the beam's tightest point.

details.didYouKnow: Six mirrors is a balance: fewer can't correct the image well enough over a wide slit, and every extra mirror throws away about 30% more light.
details.howItWorks: M5 sits close to where the bundle of rays is narrowest and hands the light to the last, largest mirror. Its shape helps fix the angle at which light finally arrives at the wafer.
keyNumbers: About 70% reflection
One of 6 projection mirrors
Roughness below a nanometre
details.madeOf: A polished low-expansion substrate with a molybdenum-silicon multilayer coating.

parts.name: Projection mirror M5

parts.description: Sixth and largest mirror, which focuses the light down onto the wafer.

details.didYouKnow: The smallest detail a lens or mirror system can print is roughly the wavelength divided by twice the numerical aperture, which is why chipmakers chase both shorter wavelengths and bigger mirrors.
details.howItWorks: M6 is the largest mirror and the last one, focusing the light down onto the wafer. Its size sets the numerical aperture, the range of angles the light arrives from, and that in turn sets how small a detail the machine can print. The newer High-NA machines use a much bigger final mirror for exactly this reason.
keyNumbers: Numerical aperture 0.33 on NXE machines
High-NA machines go to 0.55
Prints lines down to about 13 nm
details.madeOf: A large low-expansion glass-ceramic blank, polished and coated with a molybdenum-silicon multilayer.

parts.name: Projection mirror M6

parts.description: The patterned light bouncing down through the six projection mirrors to the wafer.

details.didYouKnow: The resist on the wafer needs only a small dose of EUV per square centimetre, but because so little light survives the mirrors, source power is still what limits how many wafers an hour the machine can print.
details.howItWorks: This is the patterned light leaving the reticle, bouncing down through M1 to M6 and arriving at the wafer, where it exposes the resist in the shape of the circuit. Drawn as one line here, it's really a bundle of rays carrying the image of a 26 mm wide slit.
keyNumbers: 6 reflections
Image 4 times smaller than the mask
Only a few watts reach the wafer
details.madeOf: Extreme-ultraviolet light at 13.5 nm, drawn in violet.

parts.name: EUV light (projection)

parts.description: Wafer stage under the optics: it scans the wafer through the slit of light, one chip-sized field at a time.

details.didYouKnow: ASML's twin-stage design, called TWINSCAN, arrived around 2000 and was a big part of how ASML overtook its Japanese rivals: while one wafer is exposed, the next is already being measured.
details.howItWorks: This stage carries the wafer under the projection optics and scans it through the slit of light, one chip-sized field at a time, stepping across the wafer in a grid. It floats on magnetic fields with no physical contact, and its position is tracked by encoders reading grids on the metrology frame, so every layer lands on the one beneath to within a nanometre or two.
keyNumbers: Accelerates at several g
Overlay accuracy of about 1 to 2 nm
Exposes about 160 wafers an hour on recent models
details.madeOf: A lightweight, very stiff ceramic wafer table with an electrostatic clamp, on a magnetically levitated planar motor.

parts.name: Exposure wafer stage

parts.description: Twin stage that maps the next wafer's height and position while the other is being exposed, then they swap.

details.didYouKnow: Because measuring happens in parallel with exposing, the machine can afford to measure far more carefully than it could if exposure had to wait.
details.howItWorks: While its twin is exposing one wafer, this stage carries the next wafer under the alignment and level sensors. They map exactly where the existing patterns are and how the wafer's surface rises and falls, so that during exposure the machine can steer and focus to match. Then the two stages swap places in a few seconds.
keyNumbers: Thousands of height points measured per wafer
Stages swap in a few seconds
Two stages share the same base
details.madeOf: The same kind of ceramic table and levitated motor as the exposure stage.

parts.name: Measurement wafer stage

parts.description: 300 mm silicon wafers, one on each stage, coated with resist and printed with up to a hundred or so chips each.

details.didYouKnow: The silicon is so pure that only about one atom in a billion is something other than silicon, and the wafer surface is flatter than almost anything else people make.
details.howItWorks: A wafer is a thin disc of pure silicon on which hundreds of chips are made side by side. Before it arrives here it's coated with a light-sensitive resist. Wherever the EUV hits, the resist changes chemically, and after developing, the pattern is etched into the layer beneath. A finished chip can need dozens of exposures, building up layer upon layer.
keyNumbers: 300 mm across
About 0.8 mm thick
Up to hundreds of chips per wafer, depending on size
details.madeOf: Single-crystal silicon, coated with a thin film of photoresist.

parts.name: Silicon wafers

parts.description: Optical sensors above the measurement stage that find the marks on the wafer and map its surface height.

details.didYouKnow: These sensors use ordinary visible and infrared light rather than EUV, so they can measure the wafer without exposing the resist.
details.howItWorks: The alignment sensor shines light on small marks left on the wafer by earlier layers and works out precisely where they are, so the new layer can be lined up with them. The level sensor bounces light off the wafer at a shallow angle to map its height across the surface, so the machine can keep the image in focus, which matters because the depth of focus is only tens of nanometres.
keyNumbers: Positions found to well under a nanometre
Depth of focus only tens of nanometres
Measures the wafer before every exposure
details.madeOf: Optical sensors with lasers, gratings and detectors, mounted on the metrology frame.

parts.name: Alignment & level sensors

parts.description: Robot and load-locks that bring wafers in from the coating track, warm them to the right temperature and hand them to the stages.

details.didYouKnow: Silicon grows by about 2.6 millionths of its length per degree, so a 300 mm wafer just one degree too warm would be nearly a micrometre too big, hundreds of times the alignment accuracy the machine needs.
details.howItWorks: The wafer handler takes coated wafers from the track next door, brings them through a load-lock into the vacuum and lets them settle to exactly the machine's temperature. A wafer that was even slightly warm would shrink as it cooled and its pattern would no longer line up. Robots then place each wafer on a stage and take exposed ones back out.
keyNumbers: Handles about 160 wafers an hour
Temperature matched to within hundredths of a degree
Links to the coating and developing track
details.madeOf: Vacuum robots, load-lock chambers and temperature-controlled plates inside a sealed housing.

parts.name: Wafer handler

parts.description: Fast-spinning pumps on the back of the vacuum chamber, each behind a gate valve, that sweep gas molecules out of the light path.

details.didYouKnow: A turbopump can't pump against air at normal pressure at all; its blades would be stalled by the gas, which is why every one needs a backing pump behind it.
details.howItWorks: A turbomolecular pump works like a jet engine for single molecules: stacks of angled blades spinning very fast strike gas molecules that wander in and bat them downward toward the exhaust. It only works once the pressure is already low, so smaller backing pumps in the subfab first rough the chamber down and then keep the pumps' exhausts empty through the foreline. Gate valves let a pump be shut off and swapped without letting air into the machine.
keyNumbers: Rotors spin at tens of thousands of rpm
Blade tips move at a large fraction of the speed of sound
Several pumps per machine, on different vacuum zones
details.madeOf: Aluminium-alloy rotors with many rows of blades, spinning on magnetic or ceramic ball bearings inside a steel housing, driven by their own electronics.

parts.name: Turbomolecular pumps

parts.description: Cooling water, hydrogen and nitrogen lines that run along the back of the machine and drop through the floor to the subfab.

details.didYouKnow: A fab's subfab is often as crowded as the cleanroom above it: each scanner has its own floor's worth of chillers, pumps, power cabinets and the drive laser itself.
details.howItWorks: Most of the electricity an EUV machine uses ends up as heat, so chilled water is piped in to carry it away from the source, the laser, the stages and the optics, each held at its own carefully controlled temperature. Hydrogen goes to the source vessel and the optics to keep tin and carbon off the mirrors, and clean dry nitrogen purges spaces that are opened for service. The lines drop through the raised cleanroom floor to pumps, chillers and gas cabinets in the subfab below.
keyNumbers: Cooling for roughly a megawatt of heat
Water temperature held to small fractions of a degree
Hydrogen supplied at low pressure into the vacuum
details.madeOf: Stainless steel tube with welded or sealed fittings for the gases, and insulated stainless or plastic lines for the water, with valves, filters and flow sensors along the way.

parts.name: Facility lines

parts.description: Flat bed of coils under both wafer stages; switching current through them levitates the stages and drives them in any direction.

details.didYouKnow: Because both wafer stages share one flat stator, they can drive around each other and swap places between the measurement and exposure positions in a few seconds.
details.howItWorks: Instead of rails and bearings, each wafer stage floats on magnetic fields above this flat stator. Currents switched through the coils under a stage push against magnets in its base, holding it up and driving it sideways in any direction, and even tilting it slightly. With nothing touching, there is no friction, wear or particles, and the control system can move the stage extremely smoothly while sensors on the metrology frame track it.
keyNumbers: Stages typically accelerate at several g
Gap between stage and stator of a few millimetres
Positions controlled to around a nanometre
details.madeOf: Arrays of flat copper coils potted in a stiff, water-cooled base, with the matching permanent magnets in the underside of each stage.

parts.name: Planar motor stator

summary: The machine that prints the smallest features on today's computer chips: a bus-sized vacuum scanner, made only by ASML, that blasts tin droplets into plasma to make 13.5 nm extreme-ultraviolet light, then bounces it off a chain of near-perfect mirrors to shrink a chip pattern onto a silicon wafer.
